core: what a conversion is: the moment a visitor completes a desired action, such as a purchase or a signup (working definition attributed to OpenStax Principles of Marketing 16.3 and CFI Customer Conversion Rate)
the funnel idea: awareness narrows to action, with fewer people at each step (OpenStax 16.3 sales funnel); the customer journey is a sibling topic, referenced only
four conversion types named: purchase, signup, download, inquiry — each with one line and an original example
conversion rate: the share of visitors who convert — the simple ratio (conversions ÷ visitors × 100), with an original worked example
what lifts conversion: clear calls to action, trust signals, and a simple checkout — named generally, no manipulation content
the honest note: a high conversion rate is not the same as a happy customer
the honest framing: conversion is a moment; retention is the relationship
supporting: the AMA definition of marketing frames a conversion as the exchange moment — where the value promised and the action taken meet (ama-definition-of-marketing)
social media and other digital promotion can drive visitors to a company's website, where conversions happen (OpenStax 16.2)

claims.claim: Conversions happen when a company turns a visitor into a customer; a consumer purchasing a product on a company's website and a new user signing up for a service are both conversions.

A customer conversion rate is the percentage of website visitors who perform a specific desired action on a website or landing page; the conversion action can be registering, providing contact details, making a purchase, submitting a form, calling the business, downloading a document, or signing up for a subscription.

A sales funnel is a visual representation of the customer journey from product awareness to product purchase; the number of consumers dwindles until there is an actual purchase, which represents the narrow, lower part of the funnel.
The customer conversion rate is calculated by dividing the number of people who performed a desired action in a given time frame by the total number of visitors, multiplied by 100 percent.
A conversion could be a sale, a form completion, or a click, depending on the campaign goal.
Conversion rate optimization works through design, social proof, clear display of contact information, credibility elements such as trust seals, guarantees, and removing distractions from the page.

Online marketing pages use calls to action — such as an Add to Cart button — as the point where a visitor takes the desired step; leaving a shopping cart within seconds can signal issues with that page.

Social media marketing can create traffic that links from the platform directly to a company's website, where visitors may ultimately make a purchase; campaigns are evaluated on clicks, views, and website conversions.

Marketing is the activity, set of institutions, and processes for creating, communicating, delivering, and exchanging offerings that have value for customers, clients, partners, and society at large (AMA definition); a conversion is the exchange moment.

A high conversion rate measures the moment of action, not customer satisfaction: the sources define conversions as completed actions and never as happy or loyal customers, so a business can convert visitors and still fail to retain them.

conflictingEvidence: Term-confusion caution: the phrase conversion rate has a separate, unrelated meaning in finance — the exchange ratio between two currencies (Investopedia's /terms/c/conversion-rate.asp is a currency-forex article, verified 2026-08-22, and was NOT used). This lesson uses only the marketing meaning, attributed to OpenStax 16.3 and CFI.

Definitional nuance between the two anchor sources: OpenStax 16.3 leans on customer-making actions (purchase, signup) while CFI accepts any specific desired action (registering, downloading, calling, submitting a form). The lesson's working definition resolves the difference explicitly: a conversion is any desired action the business set up, of which purchase and signup are the most common.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing, 16.3 Metrics Used to Evaluate the Success of Online Marketing
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. openstax.org blocks direct fetch; the canonical section URL was read via Wayback Machine capture 20230204195303 on 2026-08-22. Defines the sales funnel as a visual representation of the customer journey from product awareness to product purchase, with the number of consumers dwindling to the narrow lower part; defines conversions as happening when a company turns a visitor into a customer (examples: purchasing a LEGO set on a company website, signing up for TikTok); states a conversion could be a sale, a form completion, or a click; references CTA (call-to-action) buttons such as Add to Cart and shopping-cart abandonment as a page-issue signal; treats conversions as a measure of online marketing success. Facts restated in original prose per the book's no-LLM-ingestion footer.

sourceRecords.title: Customer Conversion Rate - Overview, Formula, CRO
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B reference, read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Defines customer conversion rate as the percentage of website visitors who perform a specific desired action; gives the formula (desired actions in a time frame / total visitors x 100%); lists conversion actions (registering, providing contact details, making a purchase, submitting a form, calling the business, downloading a document, signing up for a subscription); CRO levers: design, social proof, clear contact display, credibility/trust seals, guarantees, removing distractions. The lesson uses only the honest levers (clear calls to action, trust signals, simple checkout) and deliberately omits the article's urgency/scarcity tactic, which conflicts with the curriculum's no-manipulation stance. Proprietary web content: paraphrased with attribution, no text reproduced.
